items.title: Author urges people to avoid using AI note-taking devices in face-to-face meetings due to privacy and social interaction concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: I'm Begging You to Leave Your AI Note-Taker at Home
items.summary:
The article highlights concerns about the use of AI note-taking devices during face-to-face meetings, focusing on issues related to privacy, data security, and the effect on genuine social interactions. The author argues that while AI tools can be valuable in formal settings like virtual meetings, their presence in casual, in-person conversations can disrupt the natural flow and create a sense of constant surveillance.

The author explains that AI note-takers blur the traditional boundary between private and recorded conversations, turning what was once ephemeral into permanent records. This shift undermines the informal, backstage nature of personal interactions, where people feel safe to express themselves without fear of lasting documentation. The article urges individuals to consider leaving AI devices at home during in-person meetings to preserve authentic communication and protect sensitive information.

items.title: Writer critiques use of 'that sounds like AI' as a dismissive label for polished writing, arguing it reflects intellectual insecurity rather than AI detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: That Sounds Like AI: The Last Refuge of the Intellectually Insolvent
items.summary:
The article critiques the dismissive use of the phrase "that sounds like AI" to label polished writing, arguing that this accusation often reflects intellectual insecurity rather than genuine AI detection. The author, a seasoned professional writer, highlights how this phrase is frequently used as a lazy substitute for critical engagement, aimed at dehumanizing and undermining well-crafted work without substantive critique.

The piece explains that this trend reveals more about the accusers than the writing itself, suggesting that those who resort to such claims may struggle to match the quality of the writing they encounter. Rather than engaging thoughtfully, they use the accusation to mask their own limitations, turning it into a rhetorical shortcut that avoids meaningful discussion or analysis.

items.title: WebDeck launches AI-powered tool to convert PowerPoint presentations into interactive HTML with semantic content restructuring and visual editing [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WebDeck – AI-powered PPT to interactive HTML converter
items.summary:
WebDeck is an open-source tool that uses artificial intelligence to convert PowerPoint (.pptx) presentations into interactive HTML web presentations. It intelligently parses the content structure of slides, reconstructs the semantic information into native web components, and offers a visual editor for customization. This approach preserves the original presentation's intent while enabling enhanced interactivity and easier sharing through web browsers.

Unlike traditional conversion tools that simply replicate slide visuals, WebDeck treats PowerPoint files as structured content sources. It supports two conversion modes: a conservative mode that maintains the original slide structure and an enhanced mode where AI reorganizes content into dynamic web elements like cards and timelines. The tool also includes features such as full-screen presentation mode, multi-device preview, and export options for static HTML files, making it a versatile solution for modern presentation workflows.

items.title: Blog post describes AI-era FOMO as a chronic anxiety driven by rapid technological change and constant new AI tools, causing cognitive drain and identity erosion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FOMO Is the Cyberpsychosis of the AI Era
items.summary:
A blog post explores how the rapid pace of AI development has transformed the traditional fear of missing out (FOMO) into a chronic anxiety unique to the AI era. This new form of FOMO is driven by constant technological advancements and the relentless emergence of new AI tools, creating a persistent sense of falling behind despite continuous effort to keep up. The post highlights how this anxiety leads to cognitive overload and an erosion of personal identity as individuals struggle to manage the accelerating flow of information and innovation.

The article details how AI-era FOMO differs from earlier social FOMO by its basis in technological acceleration rather than social comparison, emphasizing that technology evolves faster than humans can adapt. It outlines common symptoms such as compulsive checking of news, anxiety over others' AI achievements, and the paradox of consuming vast amounts of information without producing tangible results. The post also discusses the hidden costs of this anxiety, including reduced productivity due to frequent attention switching and the psychological toll of tying self-worth to keeping pace with AI developments.

Finally, the blog suggests that this AI-driven FOMO is partly engineered by platforms that benefit from increased user engagement fueled by anxiety. It warns of the long-term consequences for mental health and creativity, urging readers to recognize and address this modern form of cyberpsychosis to regain focus and well-being in an era of rapid technological change.

items.title: Sources: China’s Kling AI nears $3 billion funding round at $18 billion valuation ahead of planned Hong Kong IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Kling AI nears US$3B round at US$18B valuation: sources
items.summary:
Kling AI, a spin-off from China's Kuaishou Technology, is nearing a $3 billion funding round that would value the company at $18 billion, according to sources. The company plans to begin the process of listing on the Hong Kong stock exchange within the next year, aiming to use the funds to expand computing infrastructure and talent acquisition amid growing competition in China's AI video generation market.

The valuation target was adjusted from an initial $20 billion as market conditions shifted. Investors in the round include Tencent, a major player in Chinese gaming and social media. Kuaishou, which competes with Douyin in the short-video space, disclosed plans to restructure Kling AI and seek external investment in a recent filing with the Hong Kong exchange.

items.originalSummary:
Could it be that Wall Street has a soft spot for refurbished internet brands? Bending Spoons, the Italian company whose stated mission is buying and overhauling left-for-dead digital businesses—such as AOL, Evernote and Vimeo—got a 40% pop on its first day as a public company on Wednesday. It was a much more impressive debut than the 4% pop scored by the other company going public on Wednesday, scooter rental firm Lime.

Both debuts, coming after SpaceX’s spectacular IPO, should reassure other companies looking to go public—including Anthropic and OpenAI—that the IPO market is well and truly open. Of course, the first day doesn’t tell us much: We’d bet Lime stock will sink in the next few days. Renting out scooters and ebikes is a tough business, given the need to spend on replacing and maintaining scooters and ebikes, relatively low margins, fierce competition and intense regulations. Ick.

items.summary:
The WSBG Terminal is a new AI-powered tool designed for German meme stock traders, offering a local alternative to the expensive Bloomberg Terminal. It provides real-time data and insights from the r/wallstreetbetsGER community, helping users track headlines, tickers, and relevant information without sifting through extensive comments. The software includes an easy installation process that automatically sets up necessary AI models to assist traders in making informed decisions.

Developed as an open-source project on GitHub, the terminal aims to be accessible despite the high costs of professional trading platforms. Users should note that the installation may trigger security warnings on Mac and Windows systems due to the lack of official developer certificates. The project encourages community contributions for bug fixes and feature enhancements, emphasizing that it is not intended as financial advice but as a tool for more efficient trading.

items.title: dupehound open-sources deterministic tool to detect AI-renamed duplicate code functions locally without AI or network access [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Open-source Deterministic Guardrails Against AI Duplicated Code
items.summary:
Dupehound is an open-source tool designed to detect duplicate code functions even after all identifiers and literals have been renamed, making it effective for codebases heavily generated by AI. It operates locally and deterministically without requiring network access, AI, or API keys, by fingerprinting the structural patterns of functions rather than their text. This approach allows dupehound to consistently identify duplicates quickly and without false positives, outperforming AI-based agents in large codebases.

The tool works by parsing functions with tree-sitter, normalizing identifiers and literals, and hashing code segments to create fingerprints that remain consistent despite renaming. It then compares these fingerprints using similarity measures and clusters duplicates efficiently. Dupehound supports multiple programming languages and offers features for scanning, history tracking, and integration with continuous integration workflows to help developers maintain cleaner codebases.

By enabling reliable detection of renamed duplicate functions offline and at scale, dupehound helps reduce redundant code and encourages reuse, which can improve code quality and maintainability in projects where AI-assisted coding is prevalent. Its deterministic and cost-free operation makes it a practical choice for developers seeking to manage duplication without relying on external AI services.

items.title: Analysis suggests AI-generated fake news site The Editorial may be a coordinated effort to poison language models with China-friendly propaganda and false journalism narratives [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: I have a theory about AI fake news site The Editorial
items.summary:
An AI-generated fake news site called The Editorial has been identified as potentially part of a coordinated effort to influence language models with China-friendly propaganda and false narratives about journalism. The site published fabricated stories, including one about a media empire replacing newspaper staff with AI, which were initially mistaken for genuine news. Analysts suggest the site aims to gain credibility by attracting links from trusted sources, thereby increasing the likelihood that language models will absorb and repeat its biased content as fact.

The Editorial's content largely focuses on topics favorable to Chinese interests, such as Taiwan and African nations where China is expanding influence. This strategy may be designed to subtly poison language models by embedding misleading information within seemingly credible articles. The site's owner, who appears to be a Finnish entrepreneur, has not clarified the intent behind the site, leaving open questions about whether this is an experiment or a deliberate disinformation campaign.

items.title: AuthSec launches unified identity and access management platform for agents and autonomous AI with authentication, MFA, OIDC federation, RBAC, and SPIFFE workload identity
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Identity Layer for Agents and Autonomous AI
items.summary:
AuthSec has introduced a unified identity and access management platform designed to handle the complete identity lifecycle for agents and autonomous AI. The platform integrates features such as authentication, multi-factor authentication (MFA), OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation, role-based access control (RBAC), SCIM provisioning, client management, external service credentials, and SPIFFE workload identity, all within a single Go service binary.

The service operates primarily as a single-tenant system using a PostgreSQL database, with optional support for multi-tenancy through an additional gRPC microservice. It offers a comprehensive API route map covering core authentication flows, WebAuthn/passkeys, client lifecycle management, OIDC provider configuration, and SPIFFE workload identity management. Optional integrations include HashiCorp Vault for secrets management, Redis for caching, and Twilio for SMS-based MFA.

AuthSec aims to simplify identity management by consolidating multiple security and authentication functions into one platform, facilitating secure and scalable access control for modern applications and autonomous systems.

Ashton Kutcher is leaving Sound Ventures, the venture capital firm he co-founded, to start a new fund with Morgan Beller focused on early-stage investments in AI infrastructure, energy, and deep tech startups. This move reflects a strategic shift from Sound Ventures' emphasis on established AI labs to backing the foundational technologies that support these companies. Kutcher will continue advising Sound Ventures, while the new firm has yet to be named.

Morgan Beller brings experience from seed-focused VC firm NFX and a leadership role in Meta's cryptocurrency project Libra, complementing Kutcher's investment background. The decision to form a new fund stems from differing views on investment stages, with Kutcher and Beller targeting earlier-stage startups compared to Sound Ventures' preference for more mature companies. Industry observers note Kutcher's consistent success as a top investor in unicorn startups, highlighting the significance of this new venture in the evolving AI investment landscape.

items.title: Introspection co-founder Roland Gavrilescu explains autoresearch feedback loops and agent recipes for self-improving AI systems and the ongoing role of humans in software development [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Autoresearch: The feedback loop behind self-improving agents
items.summary:
Roland Gavrilescu, co-founder and CEO of Introspection, discusses the concept of autoresearch, a feedback loop where AI agents help maintain and improve themselves over time. He explains how this approach involves designing effective feedback mechanisms and agent "recipes"—comprehensive frameworks that capture human expertise, evaluation methods, and system evolution—to enable self-improving AI systems while keeping humans integral to the development process.

Gavrilescu highlights the transition from focusing on individual models to managing continuous improvement loops as the core product. He emphasizes the importance of creating portable, provider-agnostic agent recipes that document the development process, including failures and decisions, to facilitate ongoing optimization. This approach aims to make AI systems more accessible, efficient, and tailored to specific environments, building on lessons from companies like Cursor and Cognition.

items.title: FactSet, Moody’s, and other financial data firms face new challenges managing AI token costs amid rising AI adoption and uncertain customer usage patterns
items.originalTitle: AI Tokenomics Come For Wall Street
items.summary:
Financial data firms like FactSet and Moody’s are navigating new challenges related to the rising costs of AI token usage as AI adoption grows in the finance sector. While these companies have reassured investors that AI tools will not replace their core data services, uncertainty around AI-related expenses and customer usage patterns is prompting questions about future revenue stability. Both FactSet and Moody’s have implemented measures to manage AI token costs internally and for their clients, with flexible pricing models to accommodate evolving consumption.

These firms have integrated AI features into their offerings and emphasize that regulated financial institutions still require licensed, verifiable data, which supports ongoing demand. However, the unpredictability of AI data consumption and token costs introduces complexity in pricing and contract structures. Despite these challenges, AI adoption is seen as a growth driver, with potential expansion into areas like wealth management, although the full impact on financial data businesses remains to be seen as the market adjusts.

items.originalSummary:
Financial data companies such as FactSet and Moody’s appear to have made progress reassuring investors that they won’t be replaced by finance-focused AI tools. But investors may have new questions these days around how the uncertainty of AI costs will affect usage of these businesses’ products.

Investors were spooked when Anthropic and others touted AI products for finance and other professions earlier this year. Companies like FactSet, Moody’s, S&P Global and LSEG, which all make money in part by selling information like market data, company financials and risk analytics, were hit by a market selloff.

Stocks have recovered at least partly since then, and the firms made a pretty compelling argument that rising usage of AI tools doesn’t hurt the value of their data. Banks, asset managers and other regulated customers still need licensed, current information that they can easily verify and audit. 

These firms have also added AI features to their products and made data available in formats customers can access through their own AI tools. Overall, they say AI adoption is positive for demand, because an AI agent can consume far more data than any human analyst. 

But things aren’t proving quite that simple. In recent months, businesses have become more focused on the rising cost of AI usage and many companies are adopting measures to keep AI spending under control. That’s raising a fresh set of AI-related questions for data sellers. 

A big question is who pays the cost of the tokens needed to run AI-powered data analysis. The answer depends on how the access to the data is structured, and whether a customer is using the data through their own AI tools or not. How much more customers are willing to pay for AI to run data analysis is another question. And like AI costs themselves, data consumption by AI tools can be unpredictable, because an agent might rerun queries or try lots of data sets. The overall picture might be unnerving for investors in a business where they’ve long prized relatively steady revenue streams. 

On Wednesday, FactSet CFO Joshua Warren said AI tokens “were not a line item that we really thought about in 2025.” Those costs are showing up in FactSet’s own spending as it uses AI internally and builds AI-powered products for customers. FactSet says it has internal controls like budgeting and model routing, and a recently expanded Google partnership gave it preferential token pricing.

When it comes to customer demand, FactSet executives noted that AI products were proving to be a source of growth and commanding richer contracts, but they also said customers are still not clear on what their own consumption will be, so want flexibility in pricing. 

“In an AI world, right now, there is a lot of value that clients are placing on that,” FactSet CEO Sanoke Viswanathan said, and the company is adding provisions for “new consumption patterns” as customers experiment.

Moody’s, for its part, appeared to be getting ahead of both sides of the cost question. In a June investor Q&A with a JPMorgan research analyst, a Moody’s executive noted that customers bear the AI token costs when they use its data through tools like Claude Enterprise, ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot. They added that Moody’s can help customers keep a lid on those costs, including by packaging its data with instructions that help AI agents use it quickly and efficiently. Moody’s also builds token costs into contracts with customers that are using its own AI tools, but it says it closely monitors those costs through routing and other measures.

To be sure, there isn’t much evidence yet that AI has moved the needle either way. Financial data businesses aren’t exactly blockbuster growth stories, but their recent growth rates still look broadly similar to before the AI scare. 

If anything, the most noticeable impact from the AI boom might be outside these companies’ data subscriptions. LSEG, which also owns the London Stock Exchange and other markets businesses, has suggested that AI is accelerating decision making and activity in general, which translates into more trading activity and risk management needs. Markets revenue jumped in the first quarter, helped by strong trading volumes. 

Meanwhile Moody’s and S&P Global have both said that a surge in debt issuance tied to AI infrastructure spending has boosted their credit ratings businesses, which make money in part when companies issue new debt and pay to have it rated.

The next question is how far into finance these companies can reach with their AI businesses. FactSet executives said on Wednesday that the wealth management industry is still in the early stages of AI adoption, but financial advisers present a big potential customer pool. That could also turn into client-facing tools for people using wealth and consumer financial services. 

New types of users could well have a very different take on AI costs and payoffs than the big existing financial customers, which could introduce further complications around fees and pricing. Meanwhile, the rest of the financial data crowd are due to report results in the coming weeks. We’ll see how the narrative continues to change.

items.title: Cloudflare requires AI companies to separate search and training crawlers by September 15 or face blocking on ad-hosting publisher sites [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cloudflare’s new policy pushes AI companies to pay for publishers’ content
items.summary:
Cloudflare has announced a new policy requiring AI companies to separate their web crawlers used for traditional search from those used for AI training and agents by September 15, 2026. If companies fail to comply, their mixed-use crawlers will be blocked by default on many ad-hosting publisher sites. This change aims to give website owners more control over how their content is accessed and used, particularly to protect intellectual property from being freely exploited by AI models.

The policy will affect new and existing Cloudflare customers, especially those using free plans, and reflects a broader shift as bot traffic surpasses human traffic online. Cloudflare is also introducing tools to help publishers monetize AI access to their content, including partnerships with AI companies like Ceramic.ai and You.com. These measures seek to create a more sustainable ecosystem by encouraging transparency and fair compensation for content usage in AI applications.

items.title: Researchers introduce MoralAltDataset to test if 15 large language models can generate and prefer moral alternatives beyond binary dilemmas, finding LLM-generated options often surpass human ones in ethical and structural quality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can LLMs Imagine Moral Alternatives Beyond Binary Dilemmas?
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MoralAltDataset, a collection of 307 moral dilemmas enhanced with compromise and reframed alternatives, to evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can generate and prefer moral options beyond traditional binary choices. Testing 15 LLMs, the study found that these models often favor compromise alternatives over original options, significantly influencing moral decision-making. The research also compared LLM-generated alternatives to human-authored ones, revealing that LLMs frequently produce options that better meet detailed structural and ethical standards.

The dataset includes both narrative Advisor dilemmas and AI-facing Agent dilemmas, reflecting diverse moral challenges. Evaluations involved pairwise preference tests and expert assessments, highlighting trade-offs between the structural quality of alternatives and their practical feasibility. This work underscores the potential of LLMs to expand moral reasoning by imagining nuanced alternatives beyond fixed dilemmas.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as moral advisors and agents, they need to address dilemmas between two competing values. However, existing research on LLMs with moral dilemmas overlooks a central aspect of human moral cognition: the ability to imagine alternatives that move beyond the given options. We introduce MoralAltDataset, a dataset of 307 moral dilemmas spanning narrative Advisor dilemmas and AI-facing Agent dilemmas, each augmented with compromise and reframed alternatives. We first examine whether humans and LLMs shift their judgments when such alternatives are introduced. Across 15 LLMs, we find that compromise alternatives are often preferred over either original option, substantially reshaping moral choice. We then evaluate the quality of LLM-generated alternatives against human-authored ones using pairwise preference and expert-based criteria. Results show that LLM-generated alternatives are often preferred and better satisfy fine-grained structural and ethical criteria, while revealing trade-offs between structural quality and practical feasibility.

items.title: Researchers introduce STEB, an open-source Style Text Embedding Benchmark covering 96 datasets in 7 languages to standardize style embedding evaluation across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: STEB: Style Text Embedding Benchmark
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Style Text Embedding Benchmark (STEB), an open-source framework designed to standardize the evaluation of style embeddings across various tasks. STEB includes 96 datasets in seven languages, covering applications such as authorship verification, authorship retrieval, AI-text detection, and linguistic feature probing. The benchmark reveals that semantic embeddings generally perform poorly on stylistic tasks and that no single style embedding excels universally across all evaluated tasks.

STEB aims to address the fragmented nature of style embedding evaluation by providing a comprehensive and consistent testing ground. The researchers have made the STEB codebase publicly available to facilitate further research and development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While semantic embeddings are rigorously evaluated on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark, the evaluation of style embeddings remains fragmented, with each work relying on their own set of tasks and datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Style Text Embedding Benchmark, a comprehensive open-source benchmark intended to standardize the evaluation of style embeddings. STEB encompasses 96 datasets across 7 languages, spanning applications such as authorship verification, authorship retrieval, AI-text detection, probing of linguistic features, and others. We find that semantic embeddings consistently fail in stylistic tasks, and that there is no style embedding that is universally superior across all tasks evaluated. We open-source the STEB code base at: https://github.com/rrivera1849/STEB.

items.title: Researchers find language models trained on fixed counterfactual explanations produce introspective explanations tracking their own behavior shifts without updated supervision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Introspective Coupling: Self-Explanation Training Tracks Behavioral Change Despite Fixed Supervision
items.summary:
Researchers have found that language models (LMs) trained to generate explanations of their predictions using fixed counterfactual explanations from earlier model checkpoints can produce introspective explanations that more accurately reflect their current behavior than the original training targets. This phenomenon, termed "introspective coupling," occurs when the training explanations remain correlated with the model's evolving behavior, allowing explanations to track behavioral changes even without updated supervision.

The study demonstrates that this introspective coupling persists across various tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and is robust to label noise. Additionally, when explanation training is combined with other post-training objectives, the explanations continue to reflect behavior shifts without needing new supervision. These findings suggest that fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can serve as scalable and generalizable signals for post-training introspection in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does training language models (LMs) to generate explanations of their predictions yield faithful introspection, rather than superficial imitation? We study LMs trained to explain which features of their inputs influenced their behavior, using models' counterfactual behavior on modified inputs as supervision. Surprisingly, we find that LMs trained on fixed counterfactual explanations derived from earlier checkpoints of themselves, or even from behaviorally similar models in different families, frequently produce explanations more faithful to their own current behaviors than to those of their training targets. This "introspective" coupling between LM explanations and behaviors occurs when training explanations remain sufficiently correlated with current behaviors over the course of training, even as behaviors themselves shift. We also show that introspective coupling tracks behavior shifts: when explanation training is provided concurrently with other post-training objectives, explanations track those shifts without requiring updated supervision. This phenomenon appears in multiple tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and is robust to label noise. Overall, our results show that even fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can provide scalable and generalizable post-training signal for introspection.

items.title: Researchers present MetaFlow, a meta-learning model that trains large language models to generate zero-shot workflows with strong generalization across tasks and operator sets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Search to Synthesis: Training LLMs as Zero-Shot Workflow Generators
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MetaFlow, a meta-learning model designed to train large language models (LLMs) to generate zero-shot workflows that generalize effectively across various tasks and operator sets. MetaFlow addresses the challenge of creating consistent, reusable workflows by learning to compose solution strategies from a given task and operator set, improving reliability and interpretability compared to instance-specific solutions. The model is trained through supervised fine-tuning on synthetic data followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, enabling it to produce robust workflows for both trained and novel tasks.

MetaFlow demonstrates strong performance across benchmarks in question answering, code generation, and mathematical reasoning, matching state-of-the-art baselines on in-domain tasks while showing remarkable zero-shot generalization to out-of-domain tasks and new operator sets. This approach offers a scalable alternative to manual workflow design, potentially enhancing the deployment and adaptability of LLMs in diverse applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across a wide range of tasks, yet their instance-specific solutions often lack the structural consistency needed for reliable deployment. Workflows that encode recurring algorithmic patterns at the task level provide a principled framework, offering robustness across instance variations, interpretable traces for debugging, and reusability across problem instances. However, manually designing such workflows requires significant expertise and effort, limiting their broader application. While automatic workflow generation could address this bottleneck, existing methods either produce instance-specific solutions without learning task-level patterns, or cannot generalize beyond their training configurations. We present MetaFlow, which casts workflow generation as a meta-learning problem: given a task and an operator set, the model learns to compose solution strategies. MetaFlow trains in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on synthetic workflow data, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) that uses execution feedback across problem instances in the task to improve end-to-end success. The resulting model produces effective workflows for trained tasks and exhibits strong generalization to untrained tasks and novel operator sets. Across benchmarks in question answering, code generation, and mathematical reasoning, MetaFlow achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines on in-domain tasks with single inference, while demonstrating remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities on out-of-domain tasks and operator sets.

items.title: Researchers study LearnStop, a cost-aware learned stopping rule for reasoning models, finding its effectiveness depends on task type and trajectory structure across 18 benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Learning to Stop Help? A Cost-Aware Study of Early Exits in Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers have examined LearnStop, a learned stopping rule designed to optimize computation in reasoning language models by predicting when to halt processing based on multiple online features. Their study across 18 benchmarks, including tasks like GSM8K and MATH-500, reveals that the effectiveness of LearnStop varies by task type and the structure of reasoning trajectories. For free-form math problems, LearnStop often outperforms simpler scalar stopping rules, while for multiple-choice and more challenging tasks, traditional scalar metrics remain competitive or superior.

The study highlights that learned stopping is particularly beneficial when many questions reach correct answers before using the full computational budget but lack a clear scalar stopping signal. The researchers provide extensive validation, including risk calibration and robustness checks, and conclude that learned stopping should be viewed as a complementary tool rather than a universal replacement for scalar exit strategies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning models spend different amounts of useful computation across instances, but it remains unclear when a learned stopping rule improves over simple confidence or convergence thresholds. We study this question with LearnStop, a hidden-state-free checkpoint stopper for reasoning language models. At fixed budget checkpoints, LearnStop probes a short answer from the current reasoning prefix and predicts prefix correctness from online features such as answer confidence, entropy, prefix vote share, answer stability, and backtracking-marker density. Across 18 task-model settings spanning GSM8K, MATH-500, MMLU-Pro, AIME-90, GPQA, Qwen3, and DeepSeek-R1 distillations, the answer is task-dependent. On free-form math, learned multi-feature stopping improves the fixed-budget frontier and often beats scalar exits: on GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, the empirical frontier reaches a post-hoc peak adapt gain of +0.157, validation-selected operating points preserve positive gains, and the paired gain over the strongest scalar baseline is +0.028. On multiple-choice and very hard settings, scalar confidence, entropy, or stability rules are competitive or stronger. We therefore frame learned stopping not as a universal replacement for scalar exits, but as a tool whose value depends on trajectory structure. We further provide validation-selected operating points, paired bootstrap tests, finite-grid lost-correct risk calibration, cost accounting under KV-fork, prefix-cache, and black-box regimes, H100 serving profiles, checkpoint-schedule sweeps, transfer analyses, and robustness checks. The main practical finding is that learned stopping is useful when many questions become correct before full budget but do not exhibit a single reliable scalar stopping signal; its benefits largely disappear when confidence or answer convergence already solves the stopping problem.

items.title: Researchers propose ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system for large language models that enforces data residency and reduces latency and costs in regulated industries [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: ComplianceGate: Classifier-Gated Multi-Tier LLM Routing for Inference in Regulated Industries
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system designed for large language models (LLMs) used in regulated industries. This system enforces compliance by routing queries based on their complexity and data sensitivity, ensuring that personally identifiable information (PII) is processed only within appropriate geographic boundaries. By directing simple queries to smaller, faster models and sensitive data to local endpoints, ComplianceGate reduces latency and costs while maintaining strict data residency compliance.

The architecture places a trained encoder classifier before any decoder inference to evaluate each query, achieving 99.2% accuracy and near-perfect PII recall with minimal inference overhead. Testing on 600 queries showed a 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and significantly higher token generation throughput compared to baseline models. This approach offers a practical path to compliance-by-design deployment of LLMs in environments with strict regulatory requirements.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31163v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models deployed in regulated industries operate under two constraints: compliance enforcement and cost efficiency. Personally identifiable information (PII) in user queries can reach model endpoints before the system determines whether that data should leave its jurisdictional boundary. Serving all queries through a single large model consumes full GPU capacity regardless of query complexity while offering no mechanism for geographic routing. Mixture-of-Experts architectures do not address this routing occurs between expert layers within the model after data has already arrived at the endpoint, with all experts loaded in memory regardless of query complexity. We propose a classifier-gated routing architecture that enforces compliance by design. A trained encoder classifier sits before any decoder inference, evaluating each query for complexity and data sensitivity, then routing it to an appropriately sized dense model in the appropriate geographic location. PII-containing queries route to local endpoints before any LLM computation begins, making data residency violations structurally impossible. Simple queries reach small, fast models at a fraction of the cost. Our evaluation on 600 queries demonstrates 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and generation throughput of 122-200 tokens/second versus 50-64 for the baseline. The encoder classifier achieves 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall at 7ms inference overhead, establishing pre-inference classification as a practical path to compliance-by-design LLM deployment.

items.title: Researchers propose failure-driven self-improvement for computer-use agents using LLMs to diagnose and patch errors, improving OpenCUA-72B success rate from 42.3% to 48.9% without extra training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning from Failure: Inference-Time Self-Improvement for Computer-Use Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a failure-driven self-improvement method for computer-use agents that utilize multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform tasks. Unlike traditional approaches that focus only on successful task completions, this method leverages failed attempts by diagnosing errors, proposing solutions, and generating code patches verified by humans to enhance the agents. Applying this technique to the OpenCUA-72B model on the OSWorld benchmark increased its success rate from 42.3% to 48.9% without additional training costs and with minimal inference overhead.

This approach complements existing success-based training pipelines by extracting valuable insights from failure cases, enabling more efficient and effective agent improvements. The results demonstrate that incorporating failure analysis into the self-improvement loop can significantly boost the performance of computer-use agents operating in verifiable environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31270v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computer-use agents, which leverage multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to operate computers and complete tasks, have attracted significant attention for their utility and versatility. A major challenge in developing these agents is collecting large-scale, high-quality trajectories. The standard approach generates synthetic data through a self-improving loop: an agent is placed in a verifiable environment and iteratively fine-tuned on its successful trajectories. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm exploits only successful trajectories and discards the failed ones, even though failures carry rich information about a model's weaknesses. In this work, we explore a complementary failure-driven self-improvement loop, a data-centric paradigm that turns failed trajectories into agent improvements. Specifically, we employ an LLM to diagnose failure modes, propose inference-time solutions, and generate code patches -- lightly verified by humans -- that upgrade the agent. We validate this approach with the state-of-the-art OpenCUA-72B model on the OSWorld benchmark, improving the success rate from 42.3% to 48.9%, a gain of 6.6 percentage points, without any additional training cost and with only modest inference overhead. Our results demonstrate that failure-driven self-improvement is a viable complement to success-based pipelines, enabling more efficient agent improvement.

items.originalTitle: Calibrating the Evaluator: Does Probability Calibration Mitigate Preference Coupling in LLM Agent Feedback Loops?
items.summary:
Researchers have found that applying probability calibration to evaluator feedback in large language model (LLM) agent training can significantly reduce evaluator preference coupling, a bias where evaluator judgments influence the agent's learned strategies. In a controlled experiment comparing standard binary feedback with confidence-calibrated feedback, calibration decreased the coupling coefficient by 20-49% and divergence measures by 45-67%, indicating less spurious preference propagation.

The study used DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the executor and GLM5.2 as the evaluator, confirming that the improvements were not due to reduced update asymmetry. The researchers have released the calibrated training protocol and recommend it as a lightweight method to mitigate evaluator bias in LLM deployment pipelines, enhancing the reliability of LLM-as-judge systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When large language model (LLM) agents adapt their behavior through evaluator feedback, systematic evaluator biases propagate into the agent's learned strategy distribution - a phenomenon termed evaluator preference coupling. Prior work has documented this coupling and established a diagnostic framework (EPC) to measure it, but has not investigated whether calibration techniques can mitigate the effect. We present the first study of evaluator calibration as mitigation: applying probability calibration to the evaluator's pairwise judgments to reduce spurious preference propagation. In a controlled within-subjects experiment (N=5) comparing standard binary TTRL (win/loss) with confidence-calibrated TTRL (probability-weighted updates) using DeepSeek-V4-Pro as executor and GLM5.2 as evaluator, we find that calibration reduces the coupling coefficient gamma by 20-49% and Jensen-Shannon divergence by 45-67%. A symmetric-LR control confirms the effect is not due to reduced update asymmetry. We release the calibrated TTRL protocol and recommend it as a lightweight mitigation for LLM-as-judge deployment pipelines.

items.title: Researcher presents ARC-AGI-2 solver using modality-driven search and holistic trace judging, achieving 72.9% accuracy on ARC Prize semi-private set, outperforming GPT-5.2 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Modality-Driven Search with Holistic Trace Judging for ARC-AGI-2
items.summary:
A new solver for the ARC-AGI-2 visual reasoning benchmark has been developed using a modality-driven search approach combined with holistic trace judging. This method treats different reasoning modalities—text, image, and code—as independent search operators and uses a judge model to evaluate all candidate reasoning traces together, improving the selection of correct answers even when they are in the minority. The solver achieved a 72.9% accuracy on the ARC Prize semi-private evaluation set, outperforming leading models like GPT-5.2 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro by a significant margin.

The solver's approach contrasts with traditional methods such as self-consistency or majority voting by preserving context and enabling better recovery of correct minority hypotheses. It also demonstrated 76.1% accuracy on the public evaluation set. The researcher has released the full source code and reported that certain techniques, like prescriptive prompting and iterative refinement, can reduce hypothesis diversity and negatively impact performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can produce fluent, internally coherent reasoning traces for abstract reasoning tasks while still being confidently wrong - making selection among candidates, not just generation, the central challenge. I present a solver for ARC-AGI-2, a few-shot visual reasoning benchmark, built around two principles: (i) treating reasoning modalities as search operators, generating diverse candidates independently across text, image, and code channels, and (ii) context-preserving holistic judging, in which a judge model jointly compares all candidate reasoning traces within a single long-context prompt. Unlike self-consistency or majority voting, this approach reliably recovers correct minority hypotheses on tasks where the modal answer is wrong. On the ARC Prize semi-private evaluation set, the solver achieves 72.9 percent at USD 38.99 per task - the highest score on the verified leaderboard at the time of writing, exceeding the best standalone frontier models, GPT-5.2 Pro at 54.2 percent and Gemini 3 Pro at 54.0 percent, by +18.7 percentage points. On the public evaluation set, it achieves 76.1 percent at USD 19.69 per task. I release the full source code and document extensive negative results, including the finding that prescriptive prompting templates and iterative refinement systematically reduce hypothesis diversity and degrade performance.

items.title: Researchers introduce QVal, a training-free testbed to cheaply evaluate dense supervision signals for long-horizon LLM agents across 21 methods and multiple environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: QVal: Cheaply Evaluating Dense Supervision Signals for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed QVal, a training-free testbed designed to evaluate dense supervision signals for long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents. QVal assesses how well a method's scoring aligns with the Q-values of a strong reference policy, enabling direct comparison of supervision signals without the need for costly training pipelines. This approach addresses the challenge of sparse outcome-only rewards by providing a way to evaluate intermediate action quality across various methods and environments.

QVal-v1.0 benchmarks 21 dense supervision methods spanning seven methodological families across four diverse environments and six open-weight model backbones, conducting over 1,200 evaluation experiments. The study found that simple prompting baselines often outperform recent dense supervision techniques, with performance clustering by method family. QVal's extensible design allows researchers to test and refine dense supervision methods efficiently before committing to full training runs, facilitating more consistent and comparable evaluations in the field.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act over long horizons, where a single trajectory can contain hundreds or thousands of actions. In these settings, outcome-only rewards provide too sparse guidance, failing to inform the model about the goodness of intermediate actions. Dense supervision methods aim to solve this problem by scoring intermediate steps, from intrinsic confidence to self-distillation and embedding similarities. However, it is common practice to evaluate them by measuring the downstream performance of a training pipeline that integrates them. This is expensive, conflates supervision quality with training engineering confounders, and renders different methodological families requiring distinct training setups incomparable. As a result, dense supervision methods are rarely benchmarked on common ground. We introduce QVal, a training-free testbed for directly evaluating dense supervision signals. Given a state-action pair, QVal measures how well a method's score is Q-aligned: whether it orders actions according to the Q-values of a strong reference-policy. This lets us compare signals before any training run and separate signal quality from other engineering choices. We instantiate QVal as QVal-v1.0, benchmarking 21 dense supervision methods across four diverse environments and seven methodological families, with over 1.2K evaluation experiments across six open-weight model backbones. We find that simple prompting baselines consistently outperform recent dense supervision methods from the literature, and that performance clusters strongly by family. These findings hold across model sizes, environments, and observation modalities. QVal is designed to be easily extensible to new environments and methods, enabling researchers to iterate on dense supervision methods before any training run.

items.title: Survey organizes AI-generated game commentary research into taxonomy of live observation, strategic analysis, and historical recall with review of methods and challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Multimodal Perception to Strategic Reasoning: A Survey on AI-Generated Game Commentary
items.summary:
A new survey paper systematically organizes the emerging field of AI-Generated Game Commentary (AI-GGC) by introducing a unified taxonomy that categorizes commentator capabilities into Live Observation, Strategic Analysis, and Historical Recall. Correspondingly, it classifies commentary into Descriptive, Analytical, and Background types. The survey reviews existing methods, datasets, and evaluation metrics, highlighting their strengths and limitations while addressing the fragmented nature of prior research.

The paper further discusses key challenges in AI-GGC and suggests promising directions for future research, aiming to advance scalable and personalized game narration through artificial intelligence. This comprehensive framework provides a foundation for unifying and guiding ongoing efforts in the development of AI-driven game commentary systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2506.17294v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence has propelled AI-Generated Game Commentary (AI-GGC) into a rapidly expanding research area, offering advantages such as scalable availability and personalized narration. However, existing studies remain fragmented, and a systematic survey that unifies prior efforts is still lacking. To bridge this gap, our survey introduces a unified framework that systematically organizes the AI-GGC landscape. We present a novel taxonomy focused on three core commentator capabilities: Live Observation, Strategic Analysis, and Historical Recall, and further categorize commentary into three corresponding types: Descriptive Commentary, Analytical Commentary, and Background Commentary. Building on this structure, we provide an in-depth review of methods, datasets, and evaluation metrics, analyzing their strengths and limitations. Finally, we highlight key challenges and point out promising directions for future research in AI-GGC.

items.title: Researchers identify shared lexical task-specific attention heads in large language models that explain prompt sensitivity and behavioral variability across instruction- and example-based prompts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Shared Lexical Task Representations Explain Behavioral Variability In LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have identified specific attention heads in large language models (LLMs) that consistently represent tasks across different prompting styles, helping to explain the models' sensitivity to how prompts are phrased. These "lexical task heads" are activated in both instruction-based and example-based prompts, influencing the model's ability to produce correct answers. Variations in model performance can be attributed to the degree of activation of these heads and the presence of competing task representations that interfere with the target task signal.

The study compares two common prompting methods—natural language instructions and few-shot examples—and finds that despite performance fluctuations, LLMs rely on shared internal mechanisms to process tasks. This insight sheds light on the internal representations driving seemingly unpredictable behaviors in LLMs, offering a clearer understanding of how prompt phrasing affects model outputs and highlighting potential avenues to improve model reliability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.22027v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: One of the most common complaints about large language models (LLMs) is their prompt sensitivity -- that is, the fact that their ability to perform a task or provide a correct answer to a question can depend unpredictably on the way the question is posed. We investigate this variation by comparing two very different but commonly-used styles of prompting: instruction-based prompts, which describe the task in natural language, and example-based prompts, which provide in-context few-shot demonstration pairs to illustrate the task. We find that, despite large variation in performance as a function of the prompt, the model engages some common underlying mechanisms across different prompts of a task. Specifically, we identify task-specific attention heads whose outputs literally describe the task -- which we dub lexical task heads -- and show that these heads are shared across prompting styles and trigger subsequent answer production. We further find that behavioral variation between prompts can be explained by the degree to which these heads are activated, and that failures are at least sometimes due to competing task representations that dilute the signal of the target task. Our results together present an increasingly clear picture of how LLMs' internal representations can explain behavior that otherwise seems idiosyncratic to users and developers.

items.title: Researchers propose GUI-AIMA, an attention-based fine-tuning framework for GUI grounding that aligns multimodal attention with patch-wise signals, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with 509k training samples [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GUI-AIMA: Aligning Intrinsic Multimodal Attention with a Context Anchor for GUI Grounding
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced GUI-AIMA, a novel attention-based fine-tuning framework designed to improve graphical user interface (GUI) grounding by aligning the intrinsic multimodal attention of large language models with patch-wise visual signals. This approach bypasses the traditional challenge of generating precise coordinates directly from visual inputs by first identifying relevant visual patches and then pinpointing exact click locations, enhancing efficiency and accuracy.

Trained on only 509,000 samples, GUI-AIMA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency and achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3-billion-parameter models across multiple benchmarks, including ScreenSpot-Pro and UI-Vision. Its coordinate-free design also supports a plug-and-play zoom-in stage, further refining its grounding capabilities. This work highlights the potential of leveraging native attention mechanisms within multimodal models to advance GUI interaction tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.00810v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding is a key capability for computer-use agents, mapping natural-language instructions to actionable regions on the screen. Existing Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) approaches typically formulate GUI grounding as a text-based coordinate generation task. However, directly generating precise coordinates from visual inputs is challenging and often data-intensive. A more intuitive strategy is to first identify instruction-relevant visual patches and then determine the exact click location within them. Motivated by recent observations that general MLLMs exhibit native grounding ability embedded in their attention maps, we propose GUI-AIMA, an attention-based and coordinate-free supervised fine-tuning framework for efficient GUI grounding. GUI-AIMA aligns the intrinsic multimodal attention of MLLMs with patch-wise grounding signals. These signals are calculated adaptively for diverse user instructions by multi-head aggregation on simplified query-visual attention matrices. Besides, its coordinate-free manner can easily integrate a plug-and-play zoom-in stage. GUI-AIMA-3B was trained with only 509k samples (around 101k screenshots), demonstrating exceptional data efficiency and verifying that light training can trigger the native grounding capability of MLLMs. It achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3B models, attaining an average accuracy of 61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 92.1% on ScreenSpot-v2, 68.1% on OSWorld-G, 79.1% on MMBench-GUI-L2, and 60.0% on UI-Vision. Project page: https://github.com/sjz5202/GUI-AIMA .

This approach bypasses the traditional challenge of generating precise coordinates directly from visual inputs by first identifying relevant visual patches and then pinpointing exact click locations, enhancing efficiency and accuracy.

Trained on only 509,000 samples, GUI-AIMA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency and achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3-billion-parameter models across multiple benchmarks, including ScreenSpot-Pro and UI-Vision. Its coordinate-free design also supports a plug-and-play zoom-in stage, further refining its grounding capabilities. This work highlights the potential of leveraging native attention mechanisms within multimodal models to advance GUI interaction tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce TaNOS framework to improve numerical reasoning robustness in expert-domain tables using operation sketches and self-supervised learning, outperforming GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro on FinQA with limited training data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Generalizing Numerical Reasoning in Table Data through Operation Sketches and Self-Supervised Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TaNOS, a continual pre-training framework designed to enhance numerical reasoning robustness in expert-domain tables. TaNOS incorporates header anonymization, operation sketches, and self-supervised pretraining to reduce reliance on superficial cues and improve structural reasoning. When applied to an 8-billion-parameter instruction-tuned model, TaNOS achieved 80.13% execution accuracy on the FinQA dataset using only 10% of the training data, outperforming fully supervised fine-tuning baselines and proprietary models like GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro.

TaNOS also demonstrated strong transferability across domains, showing minimal performance degradation in domain-shift experiments compared to standard supervised fine-tuning methods. This suggests that combining structural guidance with header-agnostic representations and correctness-guaranteed self-supervision can significantly improve the generalization and robustness of numerical reasoning models across diverse expert-domain tables.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.21495v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Numerical reasoning over expert-domain tables often exhibits high in-domain accuracy but limited robustness to domain shift. Models trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on specific datasets tend to rely on header-operation shortcuts rather than structural reasoning. We introduce TaNOS, a continual pre-training framework comprising three components: (i) header anonymization to reduce lexical memorization, (ii) operation sketches that provide minimal structural cues, and (iii) self-supervised pretraining that constructs correctness-guaranteed program-question pairs from given tables in a program-first manner. By decoupling domain semantics and numerical operation structure, TaNOS improves the transferability of numerical reasoning. Applied to an 8B instruction-tuned model, TaNOS achieves 80.13% execution accuracy on FinQA with only 10% train data, outperforming SFT baseline (73.97%) with full train data and proprietary models such as GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro. Furthermore, in the domain-shift experiments, TaNOS displays nearly-negligible cross-domain gap (<2pp) when standard SFT shows over 10pp gap. These results suggest that structural guidance with operation sketches, header-agnostic representations, and correctness-guaranteed self-supervision can improve the robustness of numerical reasoning across diverse expert-domain tables.

items.title: Researchers introduce INFUSER, an influence-guided co-training framework that improves reasoning in pretrained language models with over 20% performance gain on Olympiad and SuperGPQA benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: INFUSER: Influence-Guided Self-Evolution Improves Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed INFUSER, a novel influence-guided co-training framework that enhances reasoning capabilities in pretrained language models. INFUSER features two co-evolving components: a Generator that creates questions and reference answers from unstructured documents, and a Solver that improves by training on these generated questions. The framework uses an optimizer-aware influence score to reward the Generator for producing questions that effectively improve the Solver, resulting in over 20% performance gains on Olympiad and SuperGPQA benchmarks compared to existing self-evolution methods.

INFUSER employs a new training method called DuGRPO to handle the noisy influence scores, creating an adaptive curriculum that prioritizes questions beneficial to the Solver rather than merely difficult ones. Experiments show that an 8-billion-parameter INFUSER Generator outperforms a frozen 32-billion-parameter Generator on math and coding tasks. Additional tests confirm the necessity of each design element, and extensions demonstrate the framework's flexibility and generalizability. The code for INFUSER is publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.09052v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-evolution offers a scalable path to stronger reasoning: a pretrained language model improves itself with only minimal external supervision. Yet existing methods either depend on extensively curated or teacher-generated training data, or, when the generator runs unsupervised, reward it by a difficulty heuristic that need not improve the solver. We introduce INFUSER, an iterative co-training framework with two co-evolving roles: a Generator that drafts questions and reference golden answers from a pool of unstructured, automatically collected documents, and a Solver that improves by training on them. The solver is trained with standard correctness rewards against the generator-provided answers, while the generator is rewarded by an optimizer-aware influence score that measures whether each proposed question would actually improve the solver on the target distribution. Because this continuous, noisy influence score is poorly served by standard GRPO, we propose DuGRPO, a dual-normalized variant of GRPO, for generator training. Together, these turn the document pool into an adaptive curriculum that favors questions useful to the current solver, not just hard ones. On Qwen3-8B-Base, INFUSER outperforms strong self-evolution baselines with over 20% relative improvement on Olympiad and SuperGPQA benchmarks, and an 8B INFUSER co-evolving generator outperforms a frozen 32B thinking generator on math and coding. Ablations confirm each design choice is necessary, and two extensions, applying INFUSER to an instruction-finetuned anchor and augmenting it with rule-verifiable RLVR data, further demonstrate the flexibility and generalizability of the framework. Code is available at https://github.com/FFishy-git/INFUSER.

items.title: Researchers introduce Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation to improve long-horizon tool-use reinforcement learning by guiding credit assignment while maintaining policy gradient control, showing performance gains on AppWorld and tau^3-airline benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Keep Policy Gradient in Charge: Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation (SGCD), a method designed to improve long-horizon tool-use reinforcement learning by guiding credit assignment while maintaining policy gradient control. SGCD uses dynamic sampling of mixed successful and failed sibling rollouts, with an external large language model summarizing contrasts into a training-only credit reference, which reshapes token advantages without interfering with the actor update. This approach demonstrated improved performance on the AppWorld and tau^3-airline benchmarks compared to existing GRPO-family methods.

SGCD addresses the challenge of broadcasting trajectory-level advantages over various tokens by providing a denser and more precise credit signal through distillation used for bounded credit weighting rather than as a competing loss. Experimental results showed notable gains, such as improvements in AppWorld TGC scores and tau^3-airline evaluator scores, supporting the design principle that distillation should guide credit assignment while policy gradient remains responsible for actor updates in long-horizon tool-use agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.12634v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon tool-use reinforcement learning learns from outcome verification, but trajectory-level advantages are broadcast over reasoning, API, and answer tokens. Direct self-distillation can supply a denser signal, but in our experiments it can also destroy tool use by rehearsing teacher behavior without identifying which actions the verifier rewards. We introduce Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation (SGCD), which uses distillation for bounded credit weighting rather than as a competing actor loss. Dynamic sampling produces mixed successful and failed sibling rollouts; an external LLM summarizes their contrast into a training-only credit reference; and detached teacher/student divergence reshapes GRPO token advantages. The deployed student receives only the clean task prompt. Across AppWorld and tau^3-airline, SGCD reports higher held-out point estimates than GRPO-family comparators: AppWorld TGC improves from 42.9 to 45.6 on test_normal and from 24.7 to 27.0 on test_challenge, and tau^3-airline held-out evaluator score improves from 0.583 to 0.602. These results support a narrow design rule for long-horizon tool-use agents: use distillation to guide credit assignment while keeping policy gradient in charge of the actor update.

items.title: Researchers introduce DeXposure-Claw, an agentic system using forecast-grounded LLMs and structured evidence for decentralized finance risk supervision with regulator-aligned evaluation on five years of data [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DeXposure-Claw: An Agentic System for DeFi Risk Supervision
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DeXposure-Claw, an agentic supervision system designed to manage risks in decentralized finance (DeFi) by using forecast-grounded large language models (LLMs) combined with structured evidence. The system integrates a graph time-series foundation model to predict future exposure networks, deterministic monitors and stress scenarios to generate alerts and evidence, and confidence gates to control escalation, ultimately producing auditable supervisory tickets with clear rationales. This approach addresses the limitations of general-purpose LLM agents, which tend to overreact to weak evidence and trigger unnecessary high-stakes interventions.

To evaluate DeXposure-Claw, the team created DeXposure-Bench, a comprehensive six-axis evaluation framework that measures decision accuracy against regulator-aligned ground truth and false-intervention rates. Experiments using five years of weekly real-world data demonstrated the system's effectiveness in providing reliable and regulator-aligned risk supervision in the fast-moving DeFi environment. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.19501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks. General-purpose LLM agents fit this setting poorly: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations offer no regulator-aligned way to measure the resulting false alarms. We introduce DeXposure-Claw, a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios then turn those forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation before DeXposure-Claw emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. We further develop DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis evaluation harness, whose decision axis scores tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate. Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support our system. Code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw.

items.originalTitle: The Anthropic Fable Ban Is Over. The Battle Over How to Tame AI Has Just Begun. - WSJ
items.summary:
The Wall Street Journal reports that the ban on Anthropic's AI model has been lifted, signaling the resumption of discussions on how to regulate and control artificial intelligence. This development marks a significant moment in the ongoing debate over AI governance and safety.

The ban's end follows a period of heightened scrutiny and regulatory caution surrounding AI technologies, reflecting broader concerns about their impact and the need for effective oversight. Stakeholders are now expected to engage in renewed efforts to establish frameworks that balance innovation with ethical considerations.

This change may influence future policy decisions and industry practices as governments and companies navigate the challenges of managing advanced AI systems. The lifting of the ban could accelerate AI development while intensifying calls for responsible deployment and regulation.

items.title: Semgrep uses Anthropic’s Claude AI to automate coding fixes and feature requests from customer support tickets, currently handling a few per month with plans to scale [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Customer Support Tickets That Code
items.summary:
Semgrep, an AI cybersecurity startup, is using Anthropic's Claude AI model to automate the process of converting customer support tickets into code fixes and new features. The AI handles coding tasks in a sandboxed environment, after which human engineers test and integrate the changes into Semgrep's main application, which helps developers identify bugs and vulnerabilities. Currently, this system processes a few tickets per month, with plans to increase its usage.

This approach streamlines the traditionally slow and manual workflow of addressing customer complaints and feature requests by directly linking support tickets to code development. Semgrep's founder, Isaac Evans, highlighted that the integration of AI in this manner could significantly accelerate the response time to customer needs and improve software maintenance efficiency.

items.originalSummary:
Software developers are starting to combine the two most successful uses of large language models: coding and customer support.

Specifically, they’re using AI to automate the process of turning customer complaints about software issues or feature requests into new code. Previously, that could be a long and tedious process, which involved sending customer support tickets to a company’s support team, directing those issues to the relevant engineer, and coding up and testing a fix to the issue. 

AI cybersecurity startup Semgrep, for instance, routes customer complaints about bugs in its app or requests for new features to Anthropic’s Claude model, founder and CEO Isaac Evans said. Claude handles the fix or codes the new features in a sandboxed, isolated version of Semgrep’s app. After a human engineer tests the changes, Semgrep merges them into the real Semgrep app, which primarily helps developers scan their code for bugs and vulnerabilities, he said. Right now, Semgrep is using this approach for a handful of customer support tickets per month, but Evans expects that number to grow quickly, he said.

The company offers access to over 200 AI models while ensuring user privacy through encryption and data protection measures. With more than 3 million active users and an annualized revenue run rate exceeding $70 million, Venice AI has quickly gained traction since its launch two years ago.

The funding round was led by crypto-focused venture firm Dragonfly, with participation from Coinbase Ventures and others, reflecting the company's alignment with privacy and crypto principles championed by CEO Erik Voorhees. Venice AI provides an uncensored AI experience, allowing users to choose from various models and maintain control over their data, positioning itself as a compelling alternative to mainstream AI platforms. The company plans to use the new capital to build its own data centers and improve operational efficiency.

items.originalTitle: Gemini Spark, Google’s agentic assistant, is now available on Mac
items.summary:
Google has launched Gemini Spark, its AI agentic assistant, on Mac as part of the existing Gemini desktop app, available to AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. The update introduces real-time topic tracking and expanded integrations with apps like Google Tasks, Google Keep, Canva, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, and Zillow Rentals, enhancing its ability to assist with tasks such as organizing files, creating documents, and managing reservations or orders.

The macOS version enables Gemini Spark to work directly with files on the computer and is expected to support multi-step remote tasks via mobile devices soon. Google also introduced support for a custom Model Context Protocol, allowing users to connect additional apps to tailor the assistant to their needs, positioning Gemini Spark as a competitive option among desktop AI assistants.

items.title: Researchers launch FLARE-AI website for crowdsourced reporting and tracking of AI safety issues including malware and data leaks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: You Can Now Sound the Alarm on AI Behaving Badly
items.summary:
Researchers have launched FLARE-AI, a crowdsourced website designed to report and track safety issues in AI systems, such as malware generation, data leaks, and harmful behaviors. The platform allows users to submit reports that can be verified and routed to AI developers and organizations like MITRE, aiming to create a centralized system for identifying AI flaws.

Developed by a collaboration of 49 AI experts from 32 organizations, FLARE-AI addresses the current lack of a unified reporting mechanism for AI problems, which range from cybersecurity risks to psychological harm and bias. The initiative supports transparency and accountability in AI development, complementing recent legislative efforts in the US to establish standards and centralized databases for AI flaw reporting.

As AI systems become more powerful and autonomous, FLARE-AI could play a crucial role in managing emerging risks and encouraging safer AI deployment. The platform also faces challenges such as handling large volumes of reports and ensuring credibility, but it represents a significant step toward coordinated oversight of AI safety concerns.

items.title: Meta plans to sell excess AI compute power and models through new cloud infrastructure business, competing with AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta, like SpaceX, looks to turn excess AI compute into cash
items.summary:
Meta is planning to launch a cloud infrastructure business that will sell access to its AI compute power and models, positioning itself as a competitor to major cloud providers such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. This initiative, reportedly called Meta Compute, aims to monetize Meta's significant investments in AI data centers and infrastructure.

The move follows similar strategies by companies like SpaceX, which has leased its AI compute capacity to other firms. Meta has committed nearly $183 billion to AI infrastructure projects, including large-scale data centers in Louisiana and Ohio. Unlike some competitors, Meta has not yet generated substantial revenue from its AI models, so selling compute capacity and AI services could provide a new revenue stream.

Meta's cloud business will be led by key executives including Santosh Janardhan, Daniel Gross, and Dina Powell McCormick. This development reflects CEO Mark Zuckerberg's earlier comments about exploring cloud computing as a way to recoup investments in AI superintelligence efforts. The success of this venture will depend on sustained demand for AI compute resources and the value of data center assets.
