items.title: Researchers deploy automated pipeline to optimize enterprise AI skill descriptions, matching manual tuning accuracy while reducing engineering time 32-fold in production group chat agent [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A Single Rewrite Suffices: Empirical Lessons from Production Skill Description Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an automated pipeline to optimize natural language skill descriptions used by enterprise AI agents for routing user queries. This system addresses the issue of skill collision, where overlapping descriptions cause misrouting, by matching the accuracy of manually tuned descriptions while reducing engineering time by 32 times in a production group chat agent with nine skills. The pipeline achieved an average F1 score of 79.2%, comparable to the 79.4% from manual tuning, significantly streamlining the maintenance process as AI agents scale to handle more skills.

The study involved systematic testing on both the production system and a large tool dataset, revealing that a single large language model rewrite using false-positive and false-negative cases captures most of the improvement. Other factors such as iteration budget and training set size had minimal impact on performance. While the optimization effectively resolves skill collisions caused by overlapping descriptions, it cannot address cases where skill scopes genuinely overlap, which require architectural changes flagged by a diagnostic based on train-validation F1 score gaps.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise AI agents route user queries to specialized skills by matching queries against natural language skill descriptions. When two skills share overlapping descriptions, the routing LLM misroutes queries, a failure we term skill collision. As agents scale to dozens of skills, manually tuning descriptions to maintain routing accuracy becomes a significant engineering bottleneck. We deploy an automated description optimization pipeline on a production enterprise group chat agent (9 skills, 372 regression cases). The pipeline produces descriptions averaging 79.2% F1, matching manually tuned descriptions at 79.4% F1 (average per-skill difference -0.20%, within the 0.78% multi-seed noise floor), while reducing per-skill engineering effort from 120 minutes to 3.8 minutes (32 times speedup). We then examine which pipeline components actually drive this match. Systematic ablation on both the production system and ToolBench (16k tools) reveals that a single LLM rewrite using any available false-positive and false-negative cases captures most of the available improvement. Other design choices we tested (iteration budget, feedback signal composition, dual editing of confused pairs, and training set size) each affect final F1 by less than 0.5%. Description optimization addresses skill collisions caused by overlapping descriptions but cannot resolve cases where two skills intended scopes genuinely overlap. We identify a diagnostic (a large train-validation F1 gap) that flags the latter cases for architectural rather than text-level intervention.

items.title: Researchers introduce Indi-RomCoM benchmark to evaluate large language models on Romanized Indic-English code-mixed instructions across seven tasks and four languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Indi-RomCoM: Code-Mixed Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Romanized Indic-English Instructions
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Indi-RomCoM, a new benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on Romanized Indic-English code-mixed instructions. This benchmark covers seven instruction-following tasks across four widely spoken Indic languages and includes varying levels of code-mixing intensity. The study reveals that LLMs generally underperform on these code-mixed instructions, with performance declining as the density of code-mixing increases.

The evaluation involved a range of LLMs, including proprietary, open-weight, and Indic-focused models, tested under zero- and few-shot settings. Notably, reasoning tasks showed less performance degradation compared to detection tasks like toxicity identification, likely because generated explanations provide additional context. Indi-RomCoM aims to support the development of more inclusive multilingual AI systems that better handle the complexities of code-mixed language use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Romanized Code Mixing (RCM), where bilingual speakers fluidly blend local languages with English in Roman script, has emerged as the dominant form of communication across multilingual communities. While Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on monolingual and native-script benchmarks, their ability to follow instructions and reason over RCM-based content remains largely unexplored. To this end, we introduce the Indi-RomCoM benchmark for facilitating systematic evaluation on Indic Romanized Code-Mixed instructions. Our benchmark spans seven instruction-following tasks, four widely spoken Indic languages, and three controlled code-mixing intensity levels. We extensively evaluate a suite of LLMs covering proprietary, open-weight, and Indic-focused models under zero- and few-shot settings. LLMs consistently underperform on RCM instructions, with performance degrading as code-mixing density increases. Furthermore, reasoning tasks suffer less degradation than detection tasks (e.g., Toxicity) because the generated explanations offer necessary context. We believe Indi-RomCoM helps the community in developing inclusive multilingual systems.

items.title: Researchers use generative AI agents to automate black-box audits of personalization algorithms on X, deploying 1,120 synthetic personas to analyze content amplification after the 2024 U.S. election [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Using AI Agents to Automate Black-Box Audits of Personalization Algorithms at Scale
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a framework using generative AI agents to conduct black-box audits of personalization algorithms on online platforms. By creating 1,120 synthetic personas with fixed demographics and behaviors, they analyzed how content is personalized and amplified on X after the 2024 U.S. election. Their study revealed that X's algorithmic feed tends to amplify toxic, polarizing, political, and right-leaning content compared to the chronological feed, with variations depending on user ideology.

The AI agents were designed to interact with the platform by reasoning about content and making choices based on their assigned personas, allowing researchers to experimentally alter visible user attributes like age, gender, and location. This approach enabled counterfactual analysis of how these attributes influence content delivery. While overall demographic effects were minimal, subgroup analyses showed varying impacts on content amplification.

This work demonstrates that generative AI agents can serve as effective tools for scalable and controlled auditing of personalization algorithms, offering new insights into how user attributes affect content exposure on social media platforms.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personalization algorithms determine what content users encounter on online platforms. Auditing these systems is difficult because independent auditors have only black-box access to the algorithms, while personalization depends on users' attributes, behavior, and evolving interaction histories. Existing auditing methods face a tradeoff: studies with real users capture realistic behavior but are costly and hard to control, whereas sock-puppet audits scale more easily but often rely on scripted behavior that limits realism. Beyond this, both approaches struggle to decouple user attributes from user behavior, limiting our ability to causally understand personalization. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for black-box audits of personalization algorithms using generative AI agents as behavioral engines for synthetic accounts. Each agent is instantiated with a fixed persona, grounded in demographic and political survey data, and interacts with a platform's content by reasoning about it and choosing actions. Because behavior is fixed within each persona while platform-visible signals such as age, gender, or location can be experimentally perturbed, our design enables counterfactual auditing of how platforms respond to user attributes. As a case study, we deploy 1,120 agents on X shortly after the 2024 U.S. election, spanning 14 personas and three counterfactual conditions, collecting over 200,000 content exposures. We find that X's algorithmic feed amplifies toxic, polarizing, political, and right-leaning content relative to the chronological feed, with amplification varying sharply by user ideology. Counterfactual analyses show that demographic signals affect content delivery in persona-dependent ways: pooled effects are largely null, while subgroup-level effects vary in direction and magnitude. Our work establishes GenAI-based agents as a new tool for algorithmic auditing.

items.title: Researchers evaluate GPT-2 models trained on 'impossible' language variants, finding gradual grammatical sensitivity decline but significant generative failures linked to language non-attestation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When transformers learn "impossible" languages, what do they learn?
items.summary:
Researchers investigated how GPT-2 style transformer models perform when trained on "impossible" variants of English—languages considered unlearnable by humans. They assessed two hypotheses: whether these models show deficiencies in grammatical sensitivity or in generative production. The study found that while grammatical sensitivity declined gradually depending on the language's information locality, the models struggled significantly with generating high-quality, longer sentences in these impossible languages.

The findings suggest that the main limitation lies in the models' generative capabilities rather than grammatical understanding. This generative deficiency may explain why such impossible languages are not attested in human language, linking model behavior to linguistic non-attestation through transmission failures and production challenges.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work suggests that transformer language models show a bias towards human languages over unnatural ("impossible") languages argued to be unacquirable by humans. However, this literature has largely based these claims on differences in sample efficiency and test-set perplexity, rather than on direct evaluations of the linguistic capacities that could plausibly explain non-attestation in human languages. We evaluate two theoretically motivated linking hypotheses: impossibility arising from deficiencies in grammatical sensitivity or generative production. Using GPT-2 style models trained on perturbed "impossible" variants of English, we measure sensitivity to grammaticality using BLiMP minimal pairs, finding that model performance exhibits only gradual degradation, mediated by the language's information locality. In contrast, these models exhibited pronounced failures in generation, producing substantially fewer high-quality sentences at longer lengths. Together, these results suggest generative deficiency and transmission failures as a plausible linking hypothesis between language model behaviour and non-attestation of impossible languages.

items.title: Researchers introduce GradeSQL framework using Outcome Reward Models for test-time verification in Text-to-SQL, improving accuracy by up to 4.33% on BIRD and 2.10% on Spider benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Test-Time Verification for Text-to-SQL via Outcome Reward Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GradeSQL, a new framework that uses Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) to improve test-time verification in Text-to-SQL tasks. This approach enhances the reliability of large language models by providing learned semantic scoring functions, outperforming traditional heuristic methods like Best-of-N sampling and Majority Voting. GradeSQL demonstrated accuracy improvements of up to 4.33% on the BIRD benchmark and 2.10% on the Spider benchmark across various open-source language models.

GradeSQL trains task-specific ORMs through automated candidate generation and execution-based labeling, eliminating the need for manual annotation. The framework integrates ORMs into a verification-driven Best-of-N pipeline, showing that ORM-based selection scales effectively with larger candidate sets and yields stronger results on complex queries. The researchers have made their code, datasets, and models publicly available, offering a scalable and effective alternative for enhancing Text-to-SQL inference accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving the reliability of large language models (LLMs) at inference time is a central challenge in structured reasoning tasks such as Text-to-SQL. Common test-time inference strategies, including Best-of-N sampling and Majority Voting, rely on heuristic signals such as execution success or output frequency, which provide limited semantic discrimination across candidate outputs. In this work, we study Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) as learned semantic scoring functions for test-time verification in Text-to-SQL. While ORMs have been previously explored for test-time scaling and alignment, their application to structured query generation remains underexplored. We introduce GradeSQL, a scalable framework for training task-specific ORMs via automated candidate generation and execution-based labeling, enabling verifier training without manual annotation. We integrate ORMs into a verification-driven Best-of-N pipeline and evaluate our approach on the BIRD and Spider benchmarks across multiple open-source LLM families. ORM-based selection consistently outperforms execution-based Best-of-N and Majority Voting, with gains of up to +4.33% on BIRD and +2.10% on Spider. We further show that ORMs scale effectively with larger candidate sets and yield stronger improvements on complex queries. Overall, our results demonstrate that ORM-based verification provides a simple, effective, and scalable alternative to heuristic test-time selection strategies for Text-to-SQL. Code datasets and models are publicly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce TheraJudge and TheraAgent, multi-agent systems using human-aligned evaluation to improve therapeutic quality of mental health language models with strong clinician agreement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Training Therapeutic Judges and Multi-Agent Systems for Human-Aligned Mental Health Support
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TheraJudge and TheraAgent, a two-stage framework designed to enhance the therapeutic quality of mental health language models through human-aligned evaluation. TheraJudge is an open-source evaluator trained on human-annotated data to assess responses across seven psychological dimensions, achieving strong agreement with clinician ratings. TheraAgent uses these evaluations to iteratively refine responses via specialized roles, resulting in significant improvements in therapeutic quality and safety.

TheraJudge demonstrated high reliability, surpassing existing supervised and closed-source evaluators, particularly in critical areas such as safety, relevance, and empathy. When applied, TheraAgent improved human-rated therapeutic quality by 0.43 points on a 5-point scale and effectively corrected low-quality responses, showing a 94% recovery rate for unsafe outputs. The study highlights that aligning mental health language models with actionable human evaluations, rather than solely enhancing generation capabilities, leads to better therapeutic outcomes. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further development and use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models show promise for mental health support, yet therapeutic quality improves only when evaluation functions as an actionable control signal rather than a passive metric. We introduce a framework that formulates therapeutic response generation as a decision-refinement problem driven by multi-dimensional, human-aligned evaluation. In Stage I, we introduce TheraJudge, an open-source therapeutic evaluator trained via preference-based optimization on human-annotated data to produce reliable judgments across 7 psychological dimensions. In Stage II, we introduce TheraAgent, which operationalizes TheraJudge's evaluations through a coordinated refinement process with specialized Critic, Coach, and Therapist roles that translate evaluative signals into targeted response revisions. Empirically, TheraJudge achieves strong agreement with clinician ratings, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC = 0.87-0.95), surpassing supervised baselines and strong closed-source judges, particularly on critical dimensions such as Safety, Relevance, and Empathy. Acting on these evaluations, TheraAgent yields a +0.43 improvement in human-rated therapeutic quality (on a 5-point scale) under blind evaluation, with 96\% clinician inter-rater reliability. Low-quality responses ($\leq 3$) improve by +2.45 points with a 94\% recovery rate, demonstrating targeted correction of unsafe outputs. Overall, our results indicate that effective alignment of mental-health LLMs stems from acting on human-aligned evaluation, rather than relying solely on stronger generation. We release code at https://github.com/vis-nlp/TheraAlign.

items.title: Researchers identify deductive stereotyping in large language models and propose Fair-GCG to reduce bias and improve fairness in reasoning and generation tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wait, am I Being Fair? Characterizing Deductive Stereotyping and Mitigating It with Fair-GCG
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a bias in large language models (LLMs) called deductive stereotyping, where models apply general population statistics to individual cases, resulting in logically consistent but socially biased conclusions. To address this, they propose a reasoning-time injection framework and introduce Fair-GCG, a method to discover effective phrases that guide models toward fairness-aware reasoning. This approach improves fairness across multiple benchmarks, reduces bias in open-ended generation, and generalizes from smaller to larger models, benefiting real-world fairness-sensitive tasks.

The study provides a statistical interpretation of deductive stereotyping and demonstrates that injection phrases found by Fair-GCG enhance reasoning-level fairness and performance. This method offers a systematic way to mitigate bias in LLMs during reasoning and generation, contributing to more equitable AI applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Warning: This paper contains several toxic and offensive statements. While reasoning generally improves fairness in recent large language models (LLMs), failures persist. In this work, we identify a failure mode, deductive stereotyping, in which models apply population-level statistical regularities to individual cases, producing logically coherent yet socially biased inferences. We provide a statistical interpretation of this phenomenon. To steer models toward fairness-aware reasoning, we propose a reasoning-time injection framework. We further introduce Fair-GCG to systematically discover effective injection phrases. Injection phrases discovered by Fair-GCG improve performance across multiple fairness benchmarks, generalize from smaller to larger LLMs, improves reasoning-level fairness, reduces bias in open-ended generation, and transfer to real-world fairness-sensitive tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose Triospect, a three-dimensional statistical framework for robust AI-generated text detection, improving detection accuracy by up to 22% against 17 attack types across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Triospect: A Three-Dimensional Framework for Robust Statistical AI-Generated Text Detection Against Diverse Attacks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Triospect, a three-dimensional statistical framework designed to improve the detection of AI-generated text, particularly against various adversarial attacks. By analyzing content, core ideas, and stylistic elements, Triospect enhances detection accuracy significantly, outperforming existing methods by up to 22% across multiple benchmarks involving 17 attack types and diverse domains.

Tests on two major benchmarks demonstrated Triospect's robustness, showing improvements of 22.3% in AUROC and 13% in true positive rate on the Humanize-16K dataset after attacks, as well as 9.1% and 22% improvements respectively on the adversarial RAID dataset. This approach represents a novel statistical method to strengthen AI-generated text detection reliability. The researchers have made their data and code publicly available to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing AI-generated text detectors are vulnerable to attacks that manipulate textual characteristics. In this study, we propose a novel Triospect Detection Framework by using additional perspectives of content (core ideas) and expression (stylistic elements) within a given text. items.title: Researchers propose Training-Free Gated Reranking to reduce computational costs by up to 80% and improve few-shot learning performance by up to 2% across 8 LLMs and multiple datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Reranking Hurts: Uncertainty-Based Gating for Few-Shot Reranking
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Training-Free Gated Reranking, a method that selectively applies reranking to few-shot learning examples based on model uncertainty. This approach challenges the common assumption that reranking always enhances performance, showing instead that it can sometimes degrade results. Experiments involving eight large language models across multiple natural language understanding and machine translation datasets demonstrated that this method reduces computational costs by 15% to 80% while improving average performance by up to 2%.

The study highlights that higher computational expense does not necessarily lead to better outcomes and that reranking is most effective when focused on instances where the model exhibits high uncertainty. This finding suggests a more efficient and targeted use of reranking in few-shot learning scenarios, potentially benefiting various applications in natural language processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31087v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Few-shot selection typically assumes that reranking retrieved examples always improves performance. items.title: Researchers propose TAG-DLM, a diffusion language model integrating textual reasoning and graph message passing for text-attributed graph learning, outperforming existing methods on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TAG-DLM: Diffusion Language Models for Text-Attributed Graph Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TAG-DLM, a novel diffusion language model designed for text-attributed graph (TAG) learning that integrates textual reasoning with graph message passing. Unlike existing methods that treat text and graph data separately, TAG-DLM uses a masked diffusion language model with bidirectional attention and generative decoding to jointly process natural language descriptions and graph topology. This approach linearizes local graph neighborhoods into token sequences and incorporates graph structure through a topology attention mask, enabling effective message passing over the graph.

TAG-DLM adapts to various tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and cross-dataset transfer by simply changing the prompt, without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate that TAG-DLM outperforms graph neural networks, graph transformers, and large language model-based baselines across three TAG benchmarks and two tasks, achieving improvements of up to 3.9 points over the strongest existing methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-attributed graphs (TAGs), where each node carries a natural language description, require models to jointly reason over text and graph topology. Existing approaches often handle the two modalities separately: graph neural networks operate on shallow text features, while hybrids of LLMs and graphs use the language model mainly as a text encoder and delegate structure learning to a separate graph module. We propose method that unifies textual reasoning and graph message passing within a masked diffusion language model, a language model with bidirectional attention and generative decoding. For each graph instance, method linearises a sampled local neighbourhood into a token sequence and injects graph structure through a topology attention mask, which realises message passing over the graph. Because the diffusion language model can both interpret and generate text, the method adapts to different tasks simply by changing the prompt, supporting node classification, link prediction, and cross-dataset transfer with no target-specific fine-tuning. Experiments show that method outperforms graph neural networks, graph transformers, and LLM-based baselines on all three TAG benchmarks across two tasks, improving over the strongest baseline by up to 3.9 points.

items.title: Researchers propose Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network using speech graphs for Alzheimer's detection, achieving 90% accuracy on ADReSSo dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Gated Multi-Graph Fusion via Graph Attention Networks for Alzheimer's Disease Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network to detect Alzheimer's Disease using spontaneous speech as a non-invasive biomarker. The model transcribes audio through Automatic Speech Recognition to create semantic, dependency, and co-occurrence graphs, capturing speech characteristics in a "content-structure-flow" framework. It incorporates Pointwise Mutual Information from a normative corpus to assess narrative coherence and linguistic deviations, and uses an adaptive gated fusion mechanism to handle clinical heterogeneity. Tested on the ADReSSo dataset, the approach achieved 90% accuracy.

The study highlights the importance of the PMI-based co-occurrence graph and heterogeneity-aware gating for robust classification across diverse patient populations. The researchers have made their source code publicly available to support further development and validation in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spontaneous speech is a vital non-invasive biomarker for Alzheimer's Disease (AD), yet many systems overlook non-linear structural disruptions and clinical heterogeneity in pathological language. Notably, the co-occurrence graph leverages Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) from a normative corpus to quantify narrative logic and linguistic deviation. To address symptomatic diversity, an adaptive gated fusion mechanism dynamically integrates these views. Evaluated on the ADReSSo dataset, our model achieves 90.00% accuracy. Ablation results confirm that the PMI-based graph and heterogeneity-aware gating are essential for robust classification across diverse clinical populations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/opeacc/AD.

items.title: Researchers introduce PSALM framework to evaluate stylistic copyright infringement by large language models under EU law, revealing fine-tuning induces systematic stylistic appropriation beyond verbatim copying [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Probing Stylistic Appropriation using Large Language Models: An Evaluation Framework for Copyright Infringement under EU Law
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PSALM, a framework designed to evaluate stylistic copyright infringement by large language models (LLMs) under European Union law. Unlike existing safeguards that focus on verbatim copying, PSALM assesses broader aspects such as writing style, narrative structure, and creative elements to align with the EU's standard of substantial similarity. Applying PSALM to fine-tuned Llama 3.2 models revealed that fine-tuning leads to systematic stylistic appropriation beyond literal memorization, indicating that current protections against copyright infringement may be insufficient.

PSALM operates through ten evaluators that measure computational overlap, stylistic and content dimensions, and statutory exceptions like parody and quotation. The study found that instruction-tuned models already show baseline stylistic similarities before exposure to specific corpora, and while unlearning techniques reduce similarity, residual stylistic patterns remain detectable. This work highlights the gap between legal standards and technical detection methods, providing a tool for legally informed compliance evaluation while emphasizing the need for expert legal validation of automated similarity assessments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLM) trained on web-scale corpora generate output that may infringe copyright, yet existing technical safeguards focus narrowly on verbatim memorisation. EU copyright doctrine applies a broader standards: substantial similarity, which extends to stylistic choices, narrative structure, and creative elaboration. This mismatch between what current methods detect and what the law protects leaves a significant compliance gap. We introduce PSALM, an LLM-as-a-judge framework that operationalises EU copyright doctrine through ten evaluators assessing computational overlap, stylistic dimensions (writing style, narrative voice), content dimensions (character, plot, scene, world building), and statutory exceptions (parody, pastiche, quotation, sc\`enes \`a faire). Applying PSALM to Llama~3.2 models fine-tuned on translated historical Dutch literary works, we find that: 1) instruction-tuned models exhibit non-trivial baseline stylistic similarity prior to corpus exposure; 2) fine-tuning induces systematic stylistic appropriation across all infringement-relevant dimensions, extending beyond verbatim memorisation to abstract narrative patterns; 3) Negative Preference Optimisation unlearning substantially reduces similarity but leaves detectable residual stylistic patterns. These findings indicate that safeguards targeting literal copying alone are insufficient to mitigate broader copyright risks. PSALM provides infrastructure for auditable, legally informed compliance evaluation, though the relationship between automated similarity scores and infringement determinations requires validation by legal experts. This work bridges qualitative legal standards and quantitative technical measurement, exposing fundamental tensions between generative AI and EU intellectual property law.

items.title: Researchers propose linguistic-invariant spoofing detection using teacher-student adversarial learning and variational information bottleneck, reducing error rates by up to 36.2% across nine DF Arena datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Linguistic Bias Mitigation for Spoofing Detection via Gradient Reversal and A Variational Information Bottleneck
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new spoofing detection framework that reduces linguistic bias to improve the robustness of voice biometric systems against generative speech attacks. The approach uses a teacher-student adversarial learning model where a linguistic-aware teacher guides the student detector to minimize reliance on linguistic cues, combined with a Variational Information Bottleneck to preserve important non-linguistic features. This method achieved up to a 36.2% relative reduction in error rates across nine DF Arena datasets compared to baseline models.

The study addresses the challenge that current spoofing detectors perform well in familiar conditions but struggle to generalize to out-of-domain data due to linguistic biases learned during training. By explicitly mitigating these biases, the proposed framework enhances the generalization capability of spoofing detection systems, making them more reliable in diverse real-world scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid advancements in generative speech technology have compromised the reliability of voice biometrics. While current spoofing detectors excel when assessed under in-domain conditions, generalisation to out-of-domain settings is often poor. We show that this can be due to linguistic bias. A reliance on linguistic cues observed in training data can then compromise robustness to cross-data. We propose a linguistic-invariant spoofing detection framework utilizing teacher-student adversarial learning. The linguistic-aware teacher model, pre-trained on linguistic content of an external dataset, guides the student detector via gradient reversal to minimize the linguistic information. To prevent the inadvertent removal of non-linguistic cues, we incorporate a Variational Information Bottleneck to enable suppression of principal cues. Across nine DF Arena datasets, our method achieves up to a 36.2% relative reduction in the EER compare to the baseline.

items.summary:
Team MKC has developed a pipeline using Large Language Models (LLMs) to analyze mental health changes by examining the sequence of user posts on social media. Presented as part of the CLPsych 2026 shared task, this approach integrates post-level evaluation with user-level temporal modeling to provide a comprehensive assessment of psychological well-being.

This work addresses the growing need for scalable computational tools to support early detection and ongoing monitoring of mental health, especially given the worldwide rise in mental health disorders and limited access to professional care. By leveraging domain-specific datasets, the pipeline aims to enhance holistic mental health analysis through advanced AI techniques.

items.title: Researchers introduce FinPersona-Bench to measure mandate salience decay in autonomous financial agents using 18 LLMs with varying behavioral profiles in simulated markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FinPersona-Bench: A Benchmark for Longitudinal Psychometric Stability of Autonomous Financial Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced FinPersona-Bench, a simulation benchmark designed to measure Mandate Salience Decay (MSD) in autonomous financial agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). MSD refers to the gradual loss of influence of explicit behavioral mandates, such as capital preservation or avoiding speculative bets, as market context accumulates over time. FinPersona-Bench evaluates this phenomenon by simulating a synthetic market that separates observable prices from hidden fundamental values, allowing assessment of agent behavior across scenarios like calm markets, crashes, and speculative bubbles.

The study tested 18 leading LLMs assigned different behavioral profiles ranging from conservative to aggressive. Results showed that MSD increases over time and varies by model, with significant behavioral divergence observed during market crashes. Periodic mandate re-grounding helped conservative agents in low-signal markets but worsened outcomes for aggressive agents, indicating that effective long-term deployment of autonomous financial agents requires selective, mandate-aware adjustments tailored to agent profiles and market conditions.

These findings suggest that reliable long-horizon deployment requires selective, mandate-aware re-grounding based on agent profile and market regime.

items.title: Researchers evaluate large language models for cross-lingual relation extraction on Romanian, finding fine-tuned QLoRA improves F1 by 22 points but smaller encoders perform competitively [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cross-lingual Relation Extraction with Large Language Models: Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Fine-Tuned Evaluation on Romanian
items.summary:
Researchers have explored cross-lingual relation extraction (RE) for Romanian by translating an English benchmark dataset and evaluating large language models (LLMs) alongside smaller encoder models. They tested the Gemma 4 31B model in zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned settings using QLoRA, comparing its performance to four encoder baselines including Romanian BERT and XLM-RoBERTa variants. Fine-tuning with QLoRA significantly improved F1 scores by over 22 points and narrowed the performance gap between English and Romanian.

The study found that while the large 31B parameter model achieved the highest scores, smaller encoder models with 125M to 560M parameters performed competitively, often within a few points of the fine-tuned LLM. This suggests that for Romanian RE tasks, smaller models may offer a more practical balance of performance and computational efficiency. The researchers have made the translated dataset, evaluation code, and trained models publicly available to support further work in low-resource language processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relation extraction (RE) for low-resource languages is typically constrained by the lack of annotated corpora. We investigate the feasibility of cross-lingual RE for Romanian by combining automatic dataset translation with large language model (LLM) inference. We translate the SemEval-2010 Task 8 benchmark from English to Romanian using an LLM-based translation pipeline and evaluate Gemma 4 31B under zero-shot, few-shot, and QLoRA fine-tuned configurations, against four encoder baselines spanning 125M to 560M parameters: XLM- RoBERTa (base and large), Romanian BERT, and RoBERT- large. We assess two task formulations: relation classification with marked entities and end-to-end extraction. Our results show that Romanian incurs a 3 to 5 percentage point (pp) drop relative to English in prompt-only settings, that few-shot prompting provides marginal gains over zero-shot, and that QLoRA fine-tuning improves macro F1-Score by more than 22 percentage points in both languages while reducing the cross-lingual gap from 3.3 to 1.4pp. The encoder baselines come within 1-4pp of QLoRA Gemma on Romanian despite being 50-250 times smaller, with monolingual Romanian BERT at 125M parameters matching multilingual XLM-R at 278M. The case for using a 31B model for single-task RE on Romanian is therefore weak in deployment scenarios where compute matters. We release the translated dataset, evaluation code, and trained models.

items.title: Researchers find vision-language models overpredict shared understanding in asymmetric dialogue by conflating map content with established common ground [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Seeing Is Not Sharing: Some Vision-Language Models Overestimate Common Ground in Asymmetric Dialogue
items.summary:
Researchers have found that vision-language models (VLMs) tend to overestimate shared understanding in collaborative dialogues by confusing the presence of shared map content with actual established common ground between participants. Their study, based on 13,077 annotated reference expressions from HCRC MapTask dialogues, shows that while authentic map images improve model performance, they also cause models to over-predict alignment, treating potential shared information as if it were mutually understood.

The research involved controlled experiments manipulating dialogue context and map information access, revealing that this bias arises from task-relevant map content rather than the visual presentation itself. Models often rely on static referential cues instead of tracking how mutual understanding develops through dialogue history. This pattern was most evident in the Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model and observed to varying degrees in other architectures, indicating a common challenge in accurately modeling grounding in asymmetric dialogue.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In collaborative dialogue, shared perception does not guarantee shared interpretation. Mutual understanding must be established through interaction. We investigate whether vision-language models (VLMs) can distinguish what could be shared from what has been shared between dialogue participants through grounding. We formulate this as an interpretation-matching task on 13,077 annotated reference expressions from HCRC MapTask dialogues, and evaluate VLMs under systematically controlled manipulations of dialogue context and map-information access. Our results show that providing authentic map images improves overall performance but shifts models toward over-predicting alignment. Textual descriptions of the same map content reproduce this bias, while non-informative images suppress alignment predictions entirely, indicating that the bias is driven by task-relevant map content, not the visual channel. This improvement comes at the cost of degraded accuracy on non-aligned cases. Calibration analysis and reference-chain tracking further suggest that models rely on static referential cues on the maps rather than tracking how grounding unfolds through dialogue history. We observe these patterns most clearly in Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and, to varying degrees, in four additional models from two architecture families. In models that exhibit the bias, map content, whether presented visually or textually, is treated as evidence of mutual understanding, conflating potential with established common ground.

items.title: Researchers present CHERRY, a compute-efficient language model training approach combining selective supervision, depth compression with recurrent recovery, and fusion of compressed experts on a 1.8B-parameter Korean model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CHERRY: Compressed Hierarchical Experts with Recurrent Representational Yield
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CHERRY, a novel approach to training compute-efficient language models demonstrated on a 1.8 billion-parameter Korean model. The method combines three techniques: selective supervision focusing on the 15% of tokens carrying semantic content, depth compression with recurrent recovery to reduce model layers while maintaining performance, and fusion of compressed experts through a Mixture of Efficient Experts (MoEE) to enhance prediction accuracy. These techniques collectively improve training efficiency and model performance while reducing computational requirements.

Selective Ground Truth Token Training (SGT) concentrates learning on key tokens, achieving a 4.5-fold increase in per-supervised-token efficiency and recovering about 67% of the full-sequence loss reduction from limited supervision. Depth compression reduces a 48-layer transformer to 6 layers, restored via recurrent unrolling to match the performance of larger dense models with fewer parameters. Combining multiple compressed models as experts further improves results beyond individual models. The researchers validate these methods on the CHERRY-1.8B Korean foundation model, emphasizing the scope and limitations of their findings based on one model family and loss-based metrics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study three complementary techniques for training compute-efficient language models. (1) Selective supervision and per-token efficiency. Selective Ground Truth Token Training (SGT) concentrates supervision on the ~15% of output tokens that carry semantic payload. Through positive gradient coupling in position-shared transformer weights -- a token-level instance of auxiliary-task transfer -- the remaining 85% of unsupervised tokens still improve substantially, giving a 4.5x per-supervised-token efficiency (at the step-100 eval optimum, ~67% of the full-sequence loss reduction is recovered from 15% of the supervision). We prove that this improvement on unsupervised tokens is guaranteed whenever the gradient coupling coefficient gamma-bar = 0.72 is positive (Theorem 1), and show the effect is a property of natural-language structure: it collapses on shuffled text. (2) Depth compression with recurrent recovery. A 48-layer, 1B-parameter transformer is compressed to 6 layers (227M) by averaging adjacent layers and restored through learned recurrent unrolling. With 34 effective recurrent layers it reaches a held-out loss of 2.934, within measurement noise of a 566M dense model at 2.926 -- a 2.5x reduction in parameters. (3) Fusion of compressed experts. Assembling several compressed models as a Mixture of Efficient Experts (MoEE) with multi-token prediction improves over each single expert at comparable active parameters: a 2-expert MoEE reaches loss 2.789 versus 2.926 for the best single compressed model. We validate these techniques on CHERRY-1.8B, a Korean foundation model whose every trainable parameter derives from our own training runs. We are explicit throughout about the scope of the evidence (one model family, Korean data, loss-based metrics) and about which claims are established versus prospective.

items.title: Researchers propose a parameter-neutral transformer feed-forward layer using explicit fuzzy logic and self-forgetting quantifiers to improve grammatical licensing detection and interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Explicit Fuzzy Logic in the Feed-Forward Layer: Self-Forgetting Quantifiers Discover Legible Grammatical-Licensing Detectors
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a parameter-neutral replacement for the feed-forward sublayer in transformers, using explicit fuzzy logic operations and self-forgetting quantifiers to enhance grammatical licensing detection and interpretability. This negation-capable feed-forward network (NC-FFN) applies fuzzy set operations on sigmoid-bounded memberships, achieving competitive performance with traditional models while providing explicit logical forms for each unit. The approach addresses limitations in grammatical licensing and quantifier handling by introducing sequence quantifiers with learned forgetting rates, improving model legibility and performance on language tasks such as LAMBADA.

The new model demonstrates that grammatical licensing detectors emerge naturally within the feed-forward layers, with units responding to licensors like comparatives and negative-polarity items and carrying memory forward to predict licensed words. This interpretable mechanism offers insight into how feed-forward layers represent and license grammatical structures, resulting in a transformer model that maintains language-model quality while enhancing transparency and understanding of its internal computations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A transformer's feed-forward (FFN) sublayer materializes the distinctions attention gathers, yet gives no account of what it computes. In a parameter-neutral replacement, each hidden unit is an explicit fuzzy set operation on sigmoid-bounded [0,1] memberships: intersection A*B and set-difference A*(1-B), the latter a bounded positive negation ("A but not B") that gated/bilinear units lack -- a negation-capable FFN (NC-FFN). On N-bit parity they are the most parameter-efficient reasoning basis at shallow depth; at scale (125M, OpenWebText) NC-FFN ties the GELU baseline's perplexity, every unit carrying explicit logical form. Two limits share one cause: two-operand logic localizes to layer 0 and erodes under training, and the one robust grammatical deficit concentrates in licensing and quantifiers, beyond within-token operators. We resolve both with a small block of sequence quantifiers: a soft existential and a soft proportion, each with a per-unit learned forgetting rate from a sticky init. This recovers the deficit at epoch one (halving the wider epoch-two gap), modestly leads on LAMBADA, and makes the FFN legible: the structure now holds and migrates into depth; the decay un-learns its stickiness (median half-life ~1.5 tokens; zero latch units); and at the semantic layers the units read, without dictionary learning, as grammatical licensing detectors: each fires on a licensor (a comparative, a passive participle, a negative-polarity item) and carries its memory forward to predict the licensed word (than, by, nor). This legibility is localized and free only up to a partition (a fully Boolean FFN diverges in training), but the result is a parameter-neutral, language-model-quality transformer with a readable, interpretable-by-construction grammatical mechanism -- an account not just of what a feed-forward layer represents but how it licenses.

items.title: Researchers present first systematic evaluation of data referencing errors in large language models on tables and propose a 4B-parameter critic model improving accuracy by up to 12% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When LLMs Read Tables Carelessly: Measuring and Reducing Data Referencing Errors
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted the first systematic evaluation of data referencing errors (DREs) in large language models (LLMs) when processing tables, revealing that these errors occur across models ranging from 1.7 billion to 20 billion parameters. These errors involve incorrectly citing or omitting table values, which undermines the accuracy and reliability of intermediate reasoning steps despite the models' understanding of table structures. The study introduces a 4-billion-parameter critic model that improves answer accuracy by up to 12% through critic-based filtering and rejection sampling.

The critic model achieves an average F1 score of 78.2% in detecting both in-distribution and out-of-distribution DREs, effectively assisting larger models during inference. This approach highlights the importance of addressing data referencing errors to enhance the correctness of LLM outputs on tabular tasks and offers a promising method for improving model reliability in handling structured data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform well on table tasks, they still make data referencing errors (DREs), i.e., incorrectly citing or omitting table values, despite understanding the table structure. Beyond final-answer accuracy, DREs directly compromise the correctness and reliability of intermediate reasoning steps. Yet prior studies have only offered limited, small-scale analyses. In this work, we present the first systematic evaluation of tabular data referencing errors across different models and tasks. Our results show that DREs occur across all tested models (1.7B to 20B parameters). Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating data referencing as a critic significantly improves answer accuracy up to 12.0%, through critic-based filtering and rejection sampling. Finally, we trained a lightweight 4B-parameter critic model that achieves an average F1 score of 78.2% in detecting both in-distribution and out-of-distribution DREs, and effectively assists inference for larger models.

items.title: Researchers propose reinforcement learning with metacognitive feedback to improve uncertainty calibration and self-assessment in large language models, achieving up to 63% better performance than standard RL [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reinforcement Learning with Metacognitive Feedback Elicits Faithful Uncertainty Expression in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new approach called reinforcement learning with metacognitive feedback (RLMF) to improve large language models' (LLMs) ability to accurately assess and express their own uncertainty. This method enhances models' metacognitive skills, addressing issues like overconfidence in hallucinations and poor recognition of knowledge limits, by refining completion rankings based on the quality of the model's self-judgments and selecting valuable training data. Applied to the task of faithful calibration, RLMF achieved up to 63% better performance than standard reinforcement learning while maintaining accuracy across diverse tasks.

The approach involves a two-stage process: first calibrating the faithfulness of the models' self-reported confidence scores, then translating these into natural, context-sensitive expressions of uncertainty through targeted output editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RLMF not only improves uncertainty calibration but also enhances the models' ability to monitor and regulate their cognitive processes, positioning it as a promising paradigm for advancing LLM metacognition and alignment.

By leveraging metacognitive performance as a reinforcement learning signal, this method overcomes limitations of previous intrinsic feedback techniques, potentially leading to more trustworthy and reliable AI systems capable of better self-assessment and adaptive behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metacognition is a critical component of intelligence that describes the ability to monitor and regulate one's own cognitive processes. Yet LLMs exhibit systemic deficiencies in key metacognitive faculties: they hallucinate with high confidence, fail to recognize knowledge boundaries, and misrepresent their internal uncertainty--undermining trustworthiness and reliability. Since monitoring task performance and adapting behavior accordingly are central to metacognition, we posit that models capable of accurately judging their own performance are better positioned to improve it. We operationalize this idea via two novel mechanisms: reinforcement learning with metacognitive feedback (RLMF), a paradigm to refine completion rankings during preference optimization based on the quality of a model's self-judgments of performance, and metacognitive data selection, which uses similar self-judgments to identify high-value training examples, outperforming naive active learning. We apply these innovations to the problem of faithful calibration (FC), a task that is itself fundamentally metacognitive: the goal is to align expressed with intrinsic uncertainty, difficult even for frontier LLMs. We adopt a two-stage, decoupled approach, first using these methods to calibrate the faithfulness of models' self-reported confidence scores, then mapping to natural, context-adaptable linguistic uncertainty via targeted output editing. Extensive experiments show RLMF achieves generalizable, state-of-the-art FC on diverse tasks while preserving accuracy. Further, RLMF surpasses standard RL by up to 63% while enhancing models' ability to assess and express their own capability limits. This positions RLMF as a promising paradigm to enhance LLM metacognition toward improved abilities and alignment, and suggests metacognitive performance as an effective RL signal to overcome limits of prior intrinsic feedback methods.

items.title: Researchers propose ASR-agnostic multimodal spectrotemporal model using Mel spectrograms for early dementia detection, achieving up to 93.7% accuracy on Slovak and Spanish datasets with cross-lingual stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ASR-Agnostic Multimodal Spectrotemporal Modeling for Early Dementia Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an ASR-agnostic multimodal model that uses Mel spectrograms to detect early signs of dementia with high accuracy. The model extracts spectrotemporal displacement fields from consecutive spectrogram frames to capture shifting spectral energy patterns as biomarkers of cognitive decline. It combines these features with acoustic embeddings through a cross-attention mechanism and aggregates them using a Transformer encoder, achieving up to 93.7% accuracy on Slovak and Spanish datasets while showing cross-lingual stability.

The study trained independent models on English, Slovak, and Spanish speech corpora, each involving clinical protocols targeting cognitive domains related to daily living activities. Results showed varying performance across languages, with the Slovak model outperforming others and the English baseline affected by known recording artifacts. Ablation studies highlighted that the benefit of multimodal fusion depends on the dataset, being crucial when signals are distributed across modalities but less effective or unnecessary when one modality dominates or signals are weak.

These findings suggest that the proposed approach offers a language-independent framework for early dementia detection using speech, with implications for developing non-invasive cognitive assessment tools adaptable to different languages and recording conditions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech recruits the same executive, attentional, and working memory processes underlying instrumental activities of daily living, or IADLs, providing a non-invasive proxy for cognitive assessment. Yet most speech-based dementia detection systems depend on transcription, discard within-recording temporal structure, and are validated on a single English corpus with known recording artifacts. We propose an ASR-agnostic framework operating directly on Mel spectrograms. Our key contribution is extracting spectrotemporal displacement fields from consecutive spectrogram frames, capturing shifting spectral energy patterns as digital biomarkers of cognitive decline. These features are fused with CNN-ConvGRU acoustic embeddings via a learned cross-attention mechanism and aggregated using a Transformer encoder with learnable query pooling. A composite temporal loss enforces smoothness and contrastive coherence across segments. We train independent models on English DementiaBank, Slovak EWA-DB, and Spanish Ivanova corpora, using clinical elicitation protocols taxing IADL-relevant cognitive domains. The Slovak model achieves 83.9% accuracy, and Spanish achieves, while the English baseline yields 53.2%, confirming known artifacts. Cross-lingual ablation studies reveal distinct fusion regimes: removing cross-attention collapses Spanish performance to 53.7%, below unimodal models, while the Slovak audio encoder alone outperforms the full model, 93.7% vs. 83.9%, and all English configurations remain near chance. Thus, multimodal fusion's value is corpus-dependent: essential when signal is distributed across modalities, counterproductive when one dominates, and irrelevant when no signal exists. Auxiliary temporal losses converge to language-invariant values, indicating cross-lingual architectural stability.
